title: No formal joiner-mover-leaver (JML) process
description: Access provisioning and deprovisioning is handled ad hoc via manager requests rather than a defined, auditable workflow tied to HR events.
threat_scenario: A new hire, transfer, or termination event is missed or delayed, resulting in inappropriate access to client matter data.
existing_controls: Manual HR-to-IT handoff via Slack ticket; no automated provisioning/deprovisioning workflow.
treatment_rationale: A checklist or second-reviewer step would raise effectiveness somewhat, but it's still a manual process with the same failure mode, someone has to remember to do it. Given the low risk appetite for customer-data exposure and that this is a founding gap behind several other risks in this register (R-002, R-010), the fix needs to remove the dependency on human memory entirely, not just add redundancy to it. That's worth the engineering investment here even though a cheaper interim fix exists.
framework_mapping: SOC 2 CC6.1, CC6.2 | NIST CSF PR.AA-01, PR.AA-05

title: Incomplete offboarding leaves terminated employees with active access
description: Okta deactivation at termination is performed manually and not systematically verified; identity data confirms several terminated employees remain Active in Okta.
threat_scenario: A terminated employee retains valid SSO credentials and accesses client matter data or internal systems after separation.
existing_controls: Manager notifies IT at termination; Okta deactivation performed manually, without a closing verification step.
treatment_rationale: The identity inventory already shows this happening: at least one terminated employee remains Active in Okta with no deactivation recorded. Given Veridian's low risk appetite for customer-data exposure and that this is the highest inherent-risk item in the register at 20 (Critical), same-day automated deprovisioning tied to the HRIS termination event removes reliance on a manager remembering to notify IT, which is the exact failure mode the data already shows.
framework_mapping: SOC 2 CC6.2, CC6.3 | NIST CSF PR.AA-01

title: Shared service accounts without individual ownership
description: Several service/system accounts are shared across a team or system with no single accountable owner.
threat_scenario: An action taken under a shared account cannot be attributed to an individual, and access is never revisited because no one owns the decision to do so.
existing_controls: Service accounts are documented in an internal wiki page; no periodic ownership attestation.
treatment_rationale: A residual score of 7 is still Medium, and the core issue is accountability. If an action taken under a shared account causes a problem, there is no way to trace it back to a person. It is also lower priority than the JML-related risks in this register since it does not need new tooling. Assigning a named owner and requiring periodic attestation closes the accountability gap, and it is realistic to do alongside the higher-priority automation work rather than waiting for it.

title: Irregular user access reviews (UARs) for privileged roles
description: UARs for privileged and admin roles are performed roughly annually via manager email confirmation, with no formal cadence, tooling, or completion tracking.
threat_scenario: Privileged access that should have been revoked persists for months because no review cycle catches it.
existing_controls: Ad hoc annual UAR conducted by email; completion is not tracked centrally.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Move to a quarterly UAR cadence for privileged roles with a system of record tracking who reviewed what and when (see automation plan in Stage 5).
framework_mapping: SOC 2 CC6.1, CC6.3 | NIST CSF PR.AA-05

title: Excess vendor access to client data
description: Vendor and subprocessor access (e.g., e-discovery data processing) is provisioned at contract signing and not periodically reviewed for continued necessity or scope.
threat_scenario: A subprocessor retains broader access than its current engagement requires, widening the pool of parties that could expose client data in a breach.
existing_controls: Vendor access provisioned at contract signing; SOC 2 reports requested from major subprocessors at renewal.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Strengthen data processing addendum and indemnification language with key subprocessors so contractual liability, not just internal control, absorbs a share of this exposure while access-review process work happens in parallel.

title: Privileged session logging gaps
description: AWS API activity is logged via CloudTrail, but interactive admin sessions (SSH, kubectl, cloud console UI actions) are not separately recorded.
threat_scenario: A privileged user takes a harmful or mistaken action through an interactive session that leaves no session-level audit trail for investigation.
existing_controls: CloudTrail enabled for AWS API calls across all accounts.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Deploy session recording for interactive privileged access (SSH/kubectl/console) so API-level logging is no longer the only record of admin activity.
framework_mapping: SOC 2 CC6.3, CC7.2 | NIST CSF PR.PS-04

title: MFA coverage gap on legacy applications
description: MFA is enforced via Okta for all SSO-integrated applications, but the Legacy E-Discovery App and certain break-glass paths sit outside SSO and are not MFA-protected.
threat_scenario: A credential for one of the non-SSO applications is compromised via phishing or reuse, and there is no second factor to stop the takeover.
existing_controls: MFA enforced through Okta for all federated applications.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Extend SSO/MFA coverage to the remaining local-auth surfaces, prioritizing the Legacy E-Discovery App's admin functions first.

title: Role and privilege sprawl
description: Application and cloud roles are broadly scoped; admin-level roles are sometimes assigned at onboarding to avoid follow-up access-request tickets.
threat_scenario: A standard employee's account is compromised, and because the role is over-privileged, the blast radius includes systems or data the role never needed to touch.
existing_controls: Role definitions exist per application, but effectiveness has not been assessed and no least-privilege review has occurred.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Run a least-privilege pass on the highest-risk roles first (cloud admin, HRIS admin, billing) and right-size before tackling the full role catalog.

title: Orphaned accounts with no mapped active employee
description: Periodic manual comparison between HRIS and Okta is performed inconsistently, allowing accounts to persist without a corresponding active employee record.
threat_scenario: An orphaned account is used for unauthorized access because no one is actively responsible for noticing it should have been removed.
existing_controls: Quarterly manual export comparison between HRIS and Okta, performed inconsistently.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Automate the HRIS-to-Okta reconciliation so it runs on a fixed schedule regardless of who remembers to do it manually.

title: Mover events do not trigger access revocation
description: Internal role changes generate a request for new access but do not automatically revoke access tied to the employee's previous role.
threat_scenario: An employee who has changed departments accumulates access from both the old and new role, violating least privilege over time.
existing_controls: Role changes trigger new access requests through the standard ticketing process.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Pair every mover-triggered access grant with an explicit revocation step for the prior role's access, owned by the same ticket.

title: Admin console over-privilege on critical SaaS/cloud platforms
description: Admin-level roles on critical platforms (Okta, AWS, GitHub) are assigned broadly to IT/Security staff for convenience rather than following a tiered admin model.
threat_scenario: Compromise of any one of several broadly-privileged admin accounts grants an attacker organization-wide control over identity, infrastructure, or source code.
existing_controls: Admin role assignment is tracked informally; no tiered (standard/elevated/break-glass) admin model exists.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Introduce a tiered admin model so day-to-day work uses a lower-privilege role and full admin rights are reserved for specific, logged tasks.
framework_mapping: SOC 2 CC6.1, CC6.3 | NIST CSF PR.AA-05

title: Contractor access lifecycle not tied to engagement end date
description: Contractor access is provisioned at engagement start, but the engagement end date is not systematically linked to automatic deprovisioning.
threat_scenario: A contractor's access outlives their engagement because deprovisioning depends on someone remembering to file a request.
existing_controls: Contractor access provisioned at engagement start via standard IT ticket.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Require an end date on every contractor access grant, enforced by an automatic expiry rather than a manual follow-up.

title: SSO coverage gap on the legacy e-discovery application
description: The Legacy E-Discovery App uses local authentication for a subset of admin functions; standard user login is Okta-federated.
threat_scenario: A local admin credential on the legacy app is compromised, bypassing the SSO/MFA controls that protect the rest of the environment.
existing_controls: Standard user access is Okta-federated; local admin credentials are restricted to a small group.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: The application is expected to be replaced within the next product cycle, so full SSO integration work is not justified against a system slated for decommission.
compensating_control: DRAFT: Local admin credentials restricted to two named IT/Security staff, rotated quarterly.
escalation_path: DRAFT: If the application is still in production past the expiry date, escalate to the CTO for a go/no-go decision between funding full SSO integration and firming up the decommission timeline.

title: Break-glass emergency access lacks logging and review
description: Break-glass credentials for AWS root and Okta super-admin are stored in a shared password vault; usage is not automatically logged or reviewed after the fact.
threat_scenario: Break-glass credentials are used (legitimately or not) and no one is prompted to review what was done with them, since usage isn't tracked.
existing_controls: Break-glass credentials are stored in a shared, access-controlled password vault.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Eliminate the shared break-glass credential pattern entirely in favor of just-in-time, individually-attributed emergency access elevation with mandatory logging — removing the shared-credential exposure rather than trying to control around it.

title: SOC 2 evidence collection is scattered and untracked
description: Evidence that controls actually operated (UAR completions, access approvals, offboarding tickets) is scattered across Slack, email, and ticket systems with no centralized repository.
threat_scenario: An auditor requests evidence for a control period and Veridian cannot produce it promptly or completely, jeopardizing SOC 2 Type II attestation.
existing_controls: None — evidence exists but is not systematically collected or indexed.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Stand up a centralized system of record (see Stage 3 platform deployment) so evidence is captured as controls operate rather than reconstructed after the fact at audit time.
framework_mapping: SOC 2 CC1.1, CC4.1 | NIST CSF GV.OV-01

title: Multi-tenant data isolation has not been independently tested
description: Tenant isolation is enforced at the application data-access layer via tenant_id scoping, but no independent penetration test or isolation-specific test suite has ever validated it.
threat_scenario: A flaw in tenant-scoping logic allows one law-firm customer's matter data to be exposed to another tenant.
existing_controls: Tenant isolation enforced in application code via tenant_id scoping on all data access paths.
treatment_rationale: DRAFT: Commission an independent penetration test specifically scoped to tenant-isolation boundaries to validate the control rather than relying solely on code-level assumptions.
